social.title: Ottobar Indie Show in Charles Village
social.description: The storied indie rock venue on Howard Street books the artists two years before they're famous — small, sweaty, and the floor shakes when the bass drops.
social.bonus: Talk to the opening band after their set — they're not famous yet and they'll remember you.

social.title: Wharf Rat Pub, Fells Point
social.description: The Fells Point tap room for Oliver Brewing with dark wood, house ales on cask, and the oldest continuous tap house vibe in a neighborhood full of bars that try too hard.
social.bonus: Order something on cask — not the filtered stuff.

social.title: Peabody Library Reading Room
social.description: The George Peabody Library has a five-story atrium of cast iron balconies and 300,000 books — one of the most beautiful rooms in America, free to visit, consistently undervisited.
social.bonus: Find one book on the shelves you want to read and write down its call number.

social.title: Club Charles on Charles Street
social.description: John Waters' regular bar, unchanged since the 1950s — neon Natty Boh sign, cheap drinks, taxidermy, the most interesting crowd in Baltimore at midnight on a Saturday.
social.bonus: Stay until 1am and count how many people you recognize from somewhere else.

social.title: Max's Taphouse 100-Tap Beer Wall
social.description: 100+ taps in a Fells Point building that's been serving beer since before craft beer was a thing — the tap list is a document, the crowd is local, and nobody's pretending to be anything.
social.bonus: Ask the bartender to pick your beer based on your last three meals.

social.title: Bad Decisions Bar, Fells Point
social.description: The neon-lit Fells Point dive that earns its name on weekend nights — cheap shots, loud music, and the kind of crowd that was definitely supposed to be somewhere else by now.
social.bonus: Make one genuinely bad decision — nothing illegal, just something you'll tell people about.

social.title: Soundstage at Power Plant Live
social.description: The outdoor entertainment complex at the Inner Harbor comes alive on summer weekends — rooftop bars, live music on multiple stages, the whole city converging on one block.
social.bonus: Bar-hop through every venue in the complex before settling on one.

social.title: Night Out on The Avenue in Hampden
social.description: 36th Street in Hampden is Baltimore's most authentically weird commercial strip — bar-hop from Golden West to Holy Frijoles and feel the city's actual personality.
social.bonus: Walk the full length of The Avenue and talk to at least one shop owner or bartender about how the neighborhood has changed.

social.title: Orioles Game at Camden Yards
social.description: Camden Yards opened in 1992 and instantly became the blueprint every new ballpark has chased since — baseball here still feels like baseball is supposed to feel.
social.bonus: Buy a crab cake from the concession stand, eat it in the Eutaw Street section, and introduce yourself to whoever is standing next to you.

social.title: Happy Hour at Mount Royal Tavern
social.description: Mount Royal Tavern in Bolton Hill has been pouring cheap drinks to artists, students, and neighborhood regulars since 1966 — unpretentious, loud, and exactly right.
social.bonus: Challenge someone at the bar to a game of darts and buy a round for whoever loses.

adventure.title: National Aquarium Deep Dive
adventure.description: The Inner Harbor's anchor institution has the Atlantic coral reef tank, the Amazon river forest, dolphins, and the jellyfish gallery — go on a weekday morning to own it.
adventure.bonus: Find the weirdest-looking fish in the entire building and learn its actual name.

adventure.title: Chesapeake Bay Kayak from Canton
adventure.description: Launch from the Canton waterfront and paddle the harbor — past the Domino Sugar sign, the shipyard cranes, and under the Key Bridge with the city skyline behind you.
adventure.bonus: Paddle close enough to the Domino Sugar sign to see the ants on the lettering.

adventure.title: B&O Railroad Museum Roundhouse
adventure.description: The birthplace of American railroading — the 1884 roundhouse still contains the original locomotives and the collection spans the entire history of American rail in one enormous building.
adventure.bonus: Find the oldest locomotive in the collection and read the entire placard.

adventure.title: Edgar Allan Poe House & Grave
adventure.description: The tiny rowhouse where Poe wrote 'Berenice' and 'Morella' is preserved exactly — then walk to Westminster Hall to find his grave and the mysterious Poe Toaster's cognac bottle.
adventure.bonus: Read one Poe story in the house before you leave — they keep copies.

adventure.title: Maryland Science Center IMAX Night
adventure.description: The five-story IMAX at the Inner Harbor waterfront museum runs evening shows that fill the whole field of vision — go for something you'd never normally watch and let the screen take over.
adventure.bonus: Sit in the dead center of the middle row — the exact sweet spot for the screen geometry.

adventure.title: Fort McHenry at Dawn
adventure.description: Where the Star-Spangled Banner was written — the star-shaped fort at the mouth of the harbor is best before 8am when the flag is raised and the harbor is empty.
adventure.bonus: Get there before the flag is raised and watch it happen from the water battery.

adventure.title: Climb at Movement Timonium — Baltimore's Home Wall
adventure.description: Baltimore climbers have cut their teeth on these walls since 2002, when it opened as Earth Treks — now Movement, still the region's proving ground.
adventure.bonus: Ask a stranger to belay you on a route one grade above your limit and actually attempt it.

adventure.title: Hike the Gwynns Falls Trail Through Leakin Park
adventure.description: Seven miles of forest trail inside city limits that somehow feels like the Appalachians — Baltimore's best-kept outdoor secret.
adventure.bonus: Find the ruins of the Crimea estate deep in the park and take a photo from inside the stone walls.

adventure.title: Kayak the Inner Harbor with Waterfront Kayak
adventure.description: Paddle past the USS Constellation and the skyline from water level — the city looks completely different from a kayak.
adventure.bonus: Paddle close enough to the USS Constellation to read the hull markings without touching it.

chill.title: American Visionary Art Museum
chill.description: The Federal Hill museum dedicated to self-taught and outsider art — the giant whirligig sculpture garden on the roof is free, the main collection is the most surprising museum in Maryland.
chill.bonus: Find one piece that makes you genuinely uncomfortable and write down why.

chill.title: Federal Hill Park Overlook
chill.description: The grass hill in South Baltimore with a full panoramic view of the Inner Harbor, the downtown skyline, and the Patapsco — best at sunset with something cold.
chill.bonus: Arrive at sunset and stay until the harbor lights come on.

chill.title: Druid Hill Park Conservatory & Reservoir
chill.description: The Victorian park in Northwest Baltimore has a 19th-century glass conservatory, a reservoir loop road, and the city zoo — free to walk, wildly underappreciated.
chill.bonus: Walk the full reservoir loop and count how many different bird species you spot.

chill.title: Baltimore Museum of Art — Matisse Vault
chill.description: Free always, the BMA holds the world's largest Matisse collection — the Cone Collection wing alone is worth the trip from anywhere on the East Coast.
chill.bonus: Stand in front of one Matisse for five full minutes without moving.

chill.title: Mount Vernon Cultural Walk
chill.description: The Washington Monument predates DC's by 16 years — walk the four-block radius past the Peabody, the Walters, the clubs, and the 19th-century townhouses that define Baltimore's most beautiful neighborhood.
chill.bonus: Climb the Washington Monument column to the top — it's open on weekends for $6.

chill.title: Walters Art Museum Free Admission Drop-In
chill.description: The Walters has been free and open to the public since 1934 — 55 centuries of art from Ancient Egypt to Art Nouveau in a pair of Renaissance palaces.
chill.bonus: Find the medieval manuscripts room, pick one illuminated page, and sketch or describe it in your notes before moving on.

chill.title: Browse the Stacks at Normal's Book & Records
chill.description: Normal's in Station North has been stacking used books floor-to-ceiling alongside vinyl since 1984 — it smells like the best version of a rainy afternoon.
chill.bonus: Buy a record you've never heard solely based on the cover art and commit to listening to the full thing tonight.

chill.title: Walk Patterson Park and Climb the Pagoda
chill.description: Patterson Park's 1891 observatory pagoda gives the best elevated view of Southeast Baltimore's rowhouse rooftops and the harbor beyond.
chill.bonus: Count the distinct church steeples visible from the top of the pagoda — locals claim you can see at least seven.

chill.title: Afternoon at the Enoch Pratt Free Library Central Branch
chill.description: Maryland's grand public library opened in 1886 and its cathedral-like reading rooms are the best free afternoon you can spend in Baltimore.
chill.bonus: Find H.L. Mencken's personal collection wing and spend 20 minutes reading something from it without using your phone.

foodie.title: Woodberry Kitchen in Clipper Mill
foodie.description: Spike Gjerde's James Beard Award-winning farm-to-table landmark in a converted 19th-century mill — hyper-local sourcing, wood-fired everything, the menu changes with the season.
foodie.bonus: Ask the server where every item on your plate came from — they'll know.

foodie.title: Ekiben Asian Street Food
foodie.description: The small Station North and Federal Hill spots serve steamed buns, bibimbap bowls, and spicy pork that earned them a cult following without a single tourist knowing they existed.
foodie.bonus: Order something from the specials board only — nothing from the regular menu.

foodie.title: Pitango Gelato on Thames St
foodie.description: Small-batch, ingredient-obsessed gelato made fresh daily in the Fells Point shop — the sea salt chocolate and seasonal sorbets are the reason the line stretches outside on summer nights.
foodie.bonus: Order whatever the person behind the counter is most excited about that day.

foodie.title: Faidley's Crab Cake, Lexington Market
foodie.description: The crab cake that wins every blind tasting — jumbo lump, almost no filler, broiled not fried — eaten at the standing counter at Lexington Market the way it's been done since 1886.
foodie.bonus: Order two and eat them both — no sides, no bread, just crab.

foodie.title: Thames Street Oyster House Raw Bar
foodie.description: The serious oyster program in a cobblestone Fells Point building — a rotating selection of East and West Coast bivalves, ranked on a blackboard, eaten at the marble bar.
foodie.bonus: Order one from every region on the board and rank them without looking at the prices.

foodie.title: Nick's Fish House on the Patapsco
foodie.description: The South Baltimore waterfront dive where steamed crabs land on newspaper and the deck hangs over the Patapsco — the view is better than the address suggests.
foodie.bonus: Eat the entire dozen without using any tools — hands only.

foodie.title: Brewer's Art Belgian Beer Mansion
foodie.description: A Belgian beer bar and restaurant in a converted Charles Street mansion — the Resurrection double is brewed in-house, the upstairs dining room has exposed brick and dark wood.
foodie.bonus: Drink the Resurrection on draft — don't substitute for a bottle.

foodie.title: Bertha's Mussels in Fells Point
foodie.description: The Fells Point bar that put the 'Eat Bertha's Mussels' bumper sticker on every car in Baltimore — 30+ mussel preparations, pints of Bertha's Best Bitter, live jazz on weekends.
foodie.bonus: Order a preparation you'd never normally pick and explain why you liked it.

foodie.title: The Helmand Afghan Restaurant
foodie.description: The Afghan restaurant on Charles Street owned by Hamid Karzai's brother — the pumpkin with yogurt and meat sauce is the most famous dish in Baltimore that nobody outside Baltimore knows about.
foodie.bonus: Order the aushak dumplings AND the pumpkin — not one or the other.

foodie.title: Tasting Menu at Charleston
foodie.description: Charleston has anchored Baltimore's fine dining scene since 1997 with Cindy Wolf's Low Country–influenced cooking — this is the meal locals save for the moments that matter.
foodie.bonus: Ask the sommelier to pair one unexpected glass — something you've never heard of — and describe why it works before you taste it.

foodie.title: Steamed Crabs at LP Steamers
foodie.description: LP Steamers in Locust Point has been piling Old Bay–drenched blue crabs on brown paper tables since the neighborhood was all dockworkers — eat with your hands, no apologies.
foodie.bonus: Ask the server to crack your first crab in front of you and watch closely — then crack the rest yourself without asking for help.

foodie.title: Pit Beef at Chaps Charcoal Restaurant
foodie.description: Chaps has been grilling beef over charcoal on Pulaski Highway since 1987 — this roadside institution is Baltimore's answer to BBQ and it beats anything with a Michelin star.
foodie.bonus: Order your sandwich with tiger sauce and raw onion the local way, then finish the whole thing in the parking lot standing up.

foodie.title: Breakfast Sandwich at Atwater's Belvedere Square
foodie.description: Atwater's has been baking sourdough and feeding Baltimore proper since 2001 — the egg sandwich on house-baked bread is the city's most underrated morning ritual.
foodie.bonus: Order whatever bread they pulled from the oven that morning and eat a slice plain at the counter before your sandwich arrives.

active.title: Herring Run Park Trail — Northeast Baltimore
active.description: The 375-acre greenway in Northeast Baltimore follows Herring Run through forest and meadow — popular with birders, zero tourists, and genuinely wild for an urban park.
active.bonus: Count how many bird species you spot in one hour — the record is 47.

active.title: Inner Harbor Waterfront Bike Circuit
active.description: Bike the full Inner Harbor loop from Canton to Federal Hill on the waterfront promenade — 5 miles, waterfront the entire way, and every Baltimore landmark passes by your left shoulder.
active.bonus: Stop at every pier along the route and look back at the city from the water.

active.title: Wyman Park Strava Segment
active.description: The loop through Wyman Park, past the BMA and Johns Hopkins Homewood campus, is Baltimore's best short urban run — 2.5 miles of tree cover, hills, and architecture.
active.bonus: Run the loop twice, different directions each time.

active.title: Gwynns Falls Trail West Side Loop
active.description: The 15-mile trail along Gwynns Falls through West Baltimore connects 30 neighborhoods and passes through some of the city's oldest parks — the forest sections feel nothing like Baltimore.
active.bonus: Find Carroll Park on the route and stop at the mansion.

active.title: Jones Falls Trail — Inner Harbor to Lake Roland
active.description: The urban trail follows the Jones Falls stream 12 miles from the Inner Harbor north through Charles Village, Hampden, and Roland Park to Lake Roland — flat, continuous, and remarkable for a city trail.
active.bonus: Run or bike from the harbor to Lake Roland without stopping once.

active.title: North Central Rail Trail — Ashland to NCR
active.description: The 20-mile crushed limestone rail trail heading north from the city through the Gunpowder River valley — flat, tree-canopied, and so far removed from Baltimore it feels like a different state.
active.bonus: Ride the full length out and back — 40 miles, start before 7am.

active.title: Hampden 36th Street Avenue Walk
active.description: The Avenue in Hampden is Baltimore's most interesting block — vintage shops, independent bookstores, the hon culture in full effect, Cafe Hon, and Atomic Books where John Waters has a section.
active.bonus: Find one item at Atomic Books you'd never normally read and buy it.

active.title: Fells Point Cobblestone Walking Tour
active.description: The pre-revolutionary waterfront neighborhood on cobblestone streets has 18th-century shipwright houses, the oldest pub in Maryland, and a waterfront that's been loading cargo since 1730.
active.bonus: Find a building marker older than 1800 and photograph it.

active.title: Sunrise Rowing on the Patapsco with Baltimore Rowing Club
active.description: Baltimore Rowing Club has been launching shells from Cherry Hill since 1982 — a 6am row on the Patapsco is the kind of morning that recalibrates everything.
active.bonus: Keep your blade catches clean for a full 500-meter stretch — if you splash, you owe the cox a coffee.

active.title: Swim at Druid Hill Park Pool
active.description: Druid Hill's massive outdoor public pool is the social hub of Baltimore summers — lanes for laps, open swim for everyone, and no pretense whatsoever.
active.bonus: Swim 10 consecutive laps without stopping in the lap lane and reward yourself with the longest possible rest on the deck after.

active.title: Bike the Baltimore Waterfront Promenade
active.description: The seven-mile Waterfront Promenade connects Fells Point to Locust Point along the harbor edge — rent a Citi Bike and ride it end to end without stopping.
active.bonus: Stop at the Living Classrooms dock in Fells Point and talk to whoever is working the water — ask them what they saw this morning.

active.title: Run the Lake Montebello Loop
active.description: The 1.5-mile paved loop around Lake Montebello in Northeast Baltimore is where serious Baltimore runners train — it's flat, fast, and every lap feels like you belong here.
active.bonus: Run three full laps without stopping and nod to every runner you pass — see how many nod back.
